nameStory: Spotted spurge gets its name from the distinctive reddish or purplish spots that often appear on its small oval leaves, making it easy to pick out from other low-growing weeds. The word 'spurge' comes from an old French word meaning 'to purge,' referring to the medicinal use of these plants as laxatives in ancient times.
description: Spotted spurge is a low-growing annual weed that forms flat mats along the ground, rarely getting taller than your ankle. It has tiny oval leaves arranged in pairs along reddish stems that spread out from a central point like spokes on a wheel. The plant produces minuscule flowers and has a distinctive milky white sap that oozes out when you break a stem. It's incredibly tough and seems to thrive in the harshest spots where other plants struggle.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves about the size of your pinky nail, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, often marked with reddish or purplish spots or blotches that look like they've been dabbed with watercolor paint

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms flat, spreading mats that hug the ground tightly, with stems radiating outward from a central taproot like bicycle spokes, never standing upright

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, often reddish or pinkish stems that feel somewhat succulent and release a sticky white milky sap when broken or cut

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny inconspicuous flowers clustered in leaf joints, so small you might miss them entirely - each flower is barely the size of a pinhead and lacks petals

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small three-chambered seed capsules that split open when ripe, shooting seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop' if you listen closely

habitat: You'll find spotted spurge thriving in the toughest urban and suburban spots throughout New England - sidewalk cracks, gravel driveways, compacted garden paths, and disturbed soil along roadsides. It loves full sun and well-drained or even poor, sandy soils where most other plants can't compete. Look for it especially around railroad tracks, parking lots, and anywhere the ground gets trampled regularly.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate when soil warms in late spring, with the first small spotted leaves appearing in sunny, disturbed areas by late May.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the characteristic leaf spots are most visible and the plant forms extensive mats, flowering continuously through the heat.
seasonality.fall: Continues growing and producing seeds until the first frost kills the annual plants, turning the mats brown and brittle.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent as an annual plant, existing only as seeds in the soil waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: When spotted spurge seed pods ripen, they actually explode and can shoot their seeds up to 10 feet away - if you gently squeeze a ripe pod between your fingers, you might feel it pop and see the tiny seeds go flying!
confusionNotes: Spotted spurge is often confused with prostrate knotweed, another low-growing weed, but knotweed has alternate leaves (not opposite pairs) and lacks the milky sap. Remember: 'Spurge has sap' - break a stem and if white milk oozes out, you've found your spurge.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'prostrate spurge' by some people, don't confuse it with true prostrate spurge (Euphorbia prostrata) - they're different species. The milky sap can cause skin irritation in sensitive people and is mildly toxic, so avoid getting it in cuts or near your eyes.
compareHints: Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves. Cypress spurge grows much taller with needle-like leaves, while seaside sandmat sticks to coastal dunes and lacks the prominent leaf spots. Most other spurges in our region either grow upright or have completely different leaf shapes and growth patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
